nameStory: The swamp buttercup earned its name from its love of wet, marshy places and its bright yellow flowers that shine like little golden buttons. The "buttercup" name comes from an old children's game where you hold the flower under someone's chin - if their skin glows yellow, they supposedly love butter!
description: Swamp buttercup is a cheerful yellow wildflower that thrives in New England's wetlands and moist meadows. This low-growing perennial produces bright golden flowers with five glossy petals that seem to glow in spring sunlight. The plant typically reaches 1-2 feet tall and spreads by runners, forming patches of sunny blooms in boggy areas where many other flowers won't grow.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow flowers with 5 shiny, waxy petals that feel smooth and reflect light like tiny mirrors, typically about an inch across

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply divided leaves split into 3-5 lobes with toothed edges, feeling somewhat rough and hairy to the touch

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing plant that spreads by runners (stolons) along the ground, often forming colonies in wet areas

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, beaked seeds clustered in a round head that feels bumpy when mature, turning brown as they ripen

habitat: Swamp buttercup loves wet feet, thriving in marshes, swamps, wet meadows, and along stream banks throughout New England. You'll often find it growing alongside skunk cabbage, marsh marigold, and sedges in areas that stay moist or seasonally flooded. It tolerates both sunny and partially shaded wetlands from sea level to moderate elevations.

seasonality.spring: Bright yellow flowers bloom from April through June, creating golden carpets in wet meadows just as amphibians are most active in these same habitats.
seasonality.summer: Flowers fade and seed heads develop, while the divided leaves remain green and visible in the wetland landscape.
seasonality.fall: Seeds ripen and disperse while leaves may yellow, though the plant often stays somewhat green into late season.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to underground parts, leaving little trace above ground until spring runners emerge from the root system.

funFact: Swamp buttercup's petals have a special waxy layer that acts like a natural mirror, reflecting light to create an almost metallic shine that helps attract pollinators from far away - that's why they seem to glow even on cloudy days!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with marsh marigold, which blooms in similar wet places, but marsh marigold has much larger, rounder leaves and bigger flowers without the distinctive divided leaf pattern. Remember: swamp buttercup has deeply lobed leaves like a hand, while marsh marigold has simple heart-shaped leaves.
contextualKnowledge: Some botanists debate whether swamp buttercup is truly a separate species or just a wetland variety of bristly buttercup - this ongoing scientific discussion shows how closely related many buttercups are and why they can be tricky to tell apart.
compareHints: Unlike the common meadow buttercup which prefers drier ground and grows much taller, swamp buttercup stays low and spreads along wet soil. It differs from creeping buttercup by having more deeply divided leaves and preferring wetter habitats, while early buttercup blooms much earlier and grows in dry, rocky places rather than swamps.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's buttercups, small-flowered buttercup is unmistakable due to its tiny petals - all other buttercup species have much more prominent yellow flowers.
Among New England's buttercups, hooked buttercup is unique for its woodland habitat and tiny, pale flowers—most other buttercups prefer sunny, open areas and have much brighter, larger yellow blooms.
Among New England's many buttercup species, meadow buttercup stands out for its tall, upright growth and deeply palm-divided leaves.
Unlike meadow buttercup which grows in upright clumps, or bulbous buttercup with its swollen stem base, creeping buttercup is the only common buttercup that spreads by runners along the ground.
Among New England's many buttercup species, bulbous buttercup is the only one with that distinctive swollen stem base.
Unlike other New England buttercups that have bright, showy yellow flowers, cursed crowfoot has tiny, pale, almost insignificant blooms.
Among New England buttercups, bristly crowfoot stands out for its rough, hairy texture and pale flowers - most other buttercups have smoother leaves and bright golden-yellow blooms.
Among New England's many buttercups, yellow water-crowfoot is one of the few truly aquatic species, distinguished by its floating stems and dramatic leaf differences between air and water.
Among New England's buttercups, creeping spearwort is unique for its simple, narrow leaves - all other local buttercups have divided or lobed leaves.
Unlike the robust meadow buttercup or creeping buttercup with their typical three-lobed leaves, fen crowfoot has leaves so finely divided they look almost thread-like.

Among New England's many buttercups, early buttercup stands out for its combination of very early bloom time, preference for dry rather than moist habitats, and distinctively narrow, deeply-cut leaves.
Unlike the common meadow buttercup which grows tall and robust in fields, Allegheny Mountain buttercup stays much smaller and more delicate.
Rock buttercup stands out from other New England buttercups by having the smallest, palest flowers in the family - most other buttercups have bright golden-yellow blooms.
Among the 20+ buttercup species in New England, lesser spearwort stands out immediately because of its narrow, spear-shaped leaves – all other buttercups have lobed, divided, or rounded leaves.
Among New England's aquatic buttercups, longbeak buttercup is distinguished by its exceptionally long fruit beaks and preference for flowing water.

Among New England's many buttercups, bristly buttercup stands out primarily for its rough, hairy texture - most other species like meadow buttercup and creeping buttercup have relatively smooth stems and leaves.

Unlike terrestrial buttercups like meadow buttercup or creeping buttercup, small yellow water-crowfoot is adapted for aquatic life with thicker, more succulent leaves and a strictly prostrate growth habit.
Unlike all other New England buttercups that grow upright, Lapland buttercup stays completely flat and creeping.
Among New England's many buttercups, water-plantain spearwort is unique for its completely undivided, lance-shaped leaves - most other buttercups have deeply lobed or divided leaves.
Unlike its terrestrial buttercup cousins that have typical yellow flowers, thread-leaved water-crowfoot has white petals with yellow centers and specialized underwater foliage.
